nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Shallow, clear water lets light reach seagrass beds; Halophila ovalis can die within about 30 days if light is cut off.

nodes.name: Hot, salty shallow water
nodes.desc: The Gulf is shallow and very saline. Its seagrasses tolerate a wide range of salinity, which helps them hold the shallows.

nodes.name: Tidal flats and sabkha
nodes.desc: Tidal mudflats and salt flats line the coast of the reserve islands and host wintering waders and mangroves.

nodes.name: Seabed sediment
nodes.desc: Sandy and muddy bottom where seagrass roots, burrowing animals and buried organic matter are found.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, mangrove leaves and animal remains, returning nutrients to the sediment.

nodes.name: Narrowleaf seagrass
nodes.desc: A seagrass resident in the Persian Gulf that forms dense meadows and tolerates a wide salinity range. Dugongs favour Halodule.

nodes.name: Paddle weed
nodes.desc: A low-fibre, nitrogen-rich seagrass that dugongs prefer. It declines fast when light is lost.

nodes.name: Grey mangrove
nodes.desc: One of the few mangroves of the arid Arabian coast, growing in salt flats with aerial roots that work in flooded mud.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton and microalgae
nodes.desc: Drifting and mud-surface algae such as diatoms that feed sponges and filter-feeding flamingos.

nodes.name: White-spotted spinefoot
nodes.desc: A herbivorous fish of the Gulf that eats mainly benthic algae and some seagrass; it is trapped by local fishers.

nodes.name: Dugong
nodes.desc: Grazes seagrass, favouring Halophila and Halodule. The Gulf holds the second-largest dugong population and the UAE bans hunting.

nodes.name: Green sea turtle
nodes.desc: Adults are mostly herbivores that graze seagrasses and some algae in shallow coastal water.

nodes.name: Hawksbill sea turtle
nodes.desc: Sponges make up most of its diet, along with algae, seagrass and mangrove fruits and seeds.

nodes.name: Crabs
nodes.desc: Crabs of mudflats and mangroves feed on algae, leaf litter and dead matter and are prey for waders, fish and herons.

nodes.name: Greater flamingo
nodes.desc: Filters small prey, algae and diatoms from shallow salty mud and lagoons by stirring the mud with its feet.

nodes.name: Sponges
nodes.desc: Filter feeders of reefs and hard bottoms that strain tiny particles from the water; the main food of hawksbills.

nodes.name: Spangled emperor
nodes.desc: Eats mainly molluscs, echinoderms and crustaceans over reef, seagrass and sand. Recorded in the Persian Gulf and heavily fished there.

nodes.name: Mudskipper
nodes.desc: Amphibious fish of mudflats and mangroves that hunt small invertebrates; prey for coastal herons.

nodes.name: Western reef heron
nodes.desc: Stalks shallows for fish, crustaceans and molluscs, and regularly takes mudskippers on the coast.

nodes.name: Crab-plover
nodes.desc: A wader with a heavy bill built for crabs; it breeds in burrows in sandy banks around the Gulf.

nodes.name: Osprey
nodes.desc: Fish-eating raptor that dives feet first onto live fish; about 99% of its diet is fish.

nodes.name: Tiger shark
nodes.desc: Wide-ranging coastal predator that eats fish, sea turtles and dugongs; dugongs often carry scars from shark attacks.
